title: How Much Does Generative Engine Optimization Cost in 2026
summary: How much does generative engine optimization cost? Agency retainers run about $1,500 to $50,000+ a month with a $6,850 median, and scope explains the gap.
body_markdown:
# What Generative Engine Optimization Costs in 2026


Two GEO proposals arrive in the same week at nearly the same monthly fee. One delivers a visibility dashboard and a quarterly slide deck. The other writes pages, fixes the site and pursues coverage in the publications AI engines cite. Read side by side, the price tells you almost nothing about which one does more. Across the market, agency retainers run from about $1,500 to $50,000+ a month \[1\], and the median in the largest pricing dataset we found is $6,850 a month \[2\]. Both figures are agency-reported benchmarks.


At[Geostar](https://www.geostar.ai/) we scope and run GEO work for clients across content, technical fixes and off-site authority, so we see how much of any quote depends on the work it actually includes.


This guide covers what each way of buying GEO costs, what moves the price within a tier, and what to ask before you sign.


## GEO Pricing Ranges by Engagement Type


Generative engine optimization (GEO) is bought in five main ways. The ranges below come from two GEO agencies describing their own market, so read them as directional figures.


Engagement type Typical range What it buys


AI visibility tracking software $50 to $1,000+ per month Monitoring of where your brand appears in AI answers, with your team acting on the data


Hourly consultant $50 to $300 per hour Strategy advice or help on a single workstream


Project or audit $5,000 to $50,000 per project; one-time audit median $4,300 A defined piece of work, such as an audit, a migration or a content overhaul


Agency retainer $1,500 to $50,000+ per month; median $6,850 Ongoing strategy, implementation and reporting, with scope that varies widely


In-house team About $363,512 a year for a specialist and two writers Full control, plus the cost of hiring, tools and management


The ranges come from WebFX's GEO cost guide \[1\]. The audit median, retainer median and in-house figure come from First Page Sage's pricing report, covered in the next section.


Software suits teams that already have writers, developers and an analyst with spare hours. Hourly help and one-off projects suit companies that want a baseline or a single fix before committing. Retainers suit teams that want one partner to plan and ship the work every month, and an in-house build suits companies with enough volume to keep a full team busy.


GEO also has no standard rate card. Tenpoint Labs, another agency that sells GEO, says so directly, and the width of every range in the table reflects it. A figure from any of these sources describes the market. Your quote depends on scope.


## What a Monthly Retainer Costs at Each Tier


First Page Sage compiled 1,146 GEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) price quotes from 214 agencies between July 6 and October 2, 2026, drawn from published pricing pages, client proposals and signed contracts \[2\]. The firm sells GEO services itself, and the dataset is self-reported rather than independently audited. It is still the largest set of GEO prices we found, and it is the only one we found that reports medians by tier.


Tier Typical range Median Minimum term Deliverables per month


Starter $1,800 to $4,200 $2,950 3 months 3.4


Growth $4,500 to $11,000 $7,400 6 months 6.5


Advanced $11,000 to $22,000 $14,600 6 months 9.8


Enterprise $22,000 to $60,000+ $31,500 12 months 14.2


Every figure in this table, and every tier, industry and pricing-model statistic later in this guide, comes from that same report.


The scope changes as much as the price. Digital PR appears in 33% of Growth engagements and 71% of Advanced ones, and original research rises from 29% to 64% across the same two tiers. A move up a tier usually buys more off-site work, along with more deliverables.


Two more numbers from the dataset help put any quote in context:


- The median GEO/AEO retainer of $6,850 a month sits about 45% above the median SEO retainer of $4,740.
- Only 23% of the 214 agencies publish any GEO pricing, so public price pages show a small part of what proposals look like.


The report also records the GEO median rising 66% since Q1 2024. That is the change the dataset observed over that period, and we would not read it as a forecast for next year.


## Why the Same Work Is Priced So Differently


WebFX ties the spread in GEO pricing to website size, content needs, competition, and the number of prompts and AI platforms tracked. Across the sources and our own scoping work, six drivers come up again and again:


- AI platforms and prompts. Each engine and each tracked prompt adds monitoring and content to cover it.
- Content volume. Deliverables per month climb from 3.4 at Starter to 14.2 at Enterprise.
- Off-site authority. Digital PR, earned mentions and original research.
- Industry competition. Crowded categories need more content and more coverage to earn a citation.
- Markets covered. Multi-market coverage appears in 67% of Enterprise engagements against 24% at Advanced.
- The existing site. A site with crawl, structure or content gaps needs repair work before new content pays off.


Industry is the clearest single signal in the data. The pricing report breaks median retainers out by sector:


Industry Median monthly retainer


Financial services $9,850


B2B SaaS $8,640


Ecommerce $5,310


Home services $3,190


The pricing model shifts the number too. Across the 214 agencies, 68% sell monthly retainers (41% custom, 27% tiered), 13% price mainly as projects with a median of $14,500 per project, and 8% as one-time audits.


Off-site authority work is where the price climbs fastest. Between Growth and Advanced, digital PR goes from a third of engagements to most of them, and the median retainer roughly doubles from $7,400 to $14,600. In our work, earned coverage is the most labor-heavy line in a GEO plan, because every placement depends on an outside editor agreeing to run it. On-site changes are within your control and move faster.


## What a Monthly Number Leaves Out


Tenpoint Labs puts the comparison problem in one line: "A $12,000 retainer and a $4,000 retainer frequently contain the same five activities" \[3\]. The monthly figure on a proposal tells you what the agency charges. It does not tell you who does the work.


Most of the gap sits between two kinds of package. A reporting-and-recommendations package hands your team a dashboard and a list of changes. An execution package, the model we describe in our explainer on[what an SEO and GEO agency does](https://www.geostar.ai/blog/what-is-an-seo-geo-agency) , includes the people who write the pages, ship the technical fixes and pursue the coverage. Dashboard and report vendors price the first kind; we sell the second, because a recommendation that nobody implements does not change what AI engines cite.


WebFX's advice for comparing quotes is to line them up on the same units: the AI platforms covered, the number of tracked prompts, whether tracking software is included, and how the provider bills. We would add implementation and measurement to that list. These five questions separate a thin proposal from a complete one:


Question to ask What a thin answer looks like What a complete answer includes


Which AI platforms are covered? One engine, usually ChatGPT Named engines, such as ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini and Perplexity


How many prompts are tracked, and who picks them? A prompt count with no list A written prompt list tied to buyer questions, with a process for changing it


Is tracking software bundled? A separate subscription added later Tracking included, or priced as its own line


Who does the implementation? Recommendations handed to your team Named deliverables: pages written, fixes shipped, placements pursued


How is success measured? Mention counts in a monthly report A baseline, repeated runs across engines, and a link to leads and revenue


A proposal that answers all five in writing is one you can price against another. When the answers are vague, the lower quote often buys less work.


## Where GEO Spend Does Not Pay Back


Some line items sound technical and still lack evidence. Schema markup is the clearest example. Ahrefs tracked 1,885 pages that added JSON-LD schema between August 2025 and March 2026 against 4,000 matched control pages \[4\]. It found no meaningful citation uplift on Google AI Mode (+2.4%) or ChatGPT (+2.2%), and a small decline on Google AI Overviews (-4.6%) at a time when both groups were declining.


The study has limits worth stating. The pages were already heavily cited, the measurement window was 30 days, and it covered JSON-LD only. It does not show that schema is useless for every site. It does show that a package built mainly on adding markup is a weak place to put a GEO budget.


The research base for GEO methods is real but narrow. The foundational paper that introduced the term reports visibility gains of up to 40% in generative engine responses in experimental settings, with results that vary by domain \[5\]. It measures content methods in controlled tests and says nothing about pricing or typical return on spend.


AI answers are also non-deterministic. The same prompt can return different sources on different runs, so results arrive in stages and need repeated measurement. Treat these as price red flags:


- Guaranteed citations, or a promised placement in a named AI answer.
- A package priced mainly around schema or other markup.
- No baseline measurement before the work starts.
- Reporting built on a single run of each prompt.


## Software, In-House, or Agency: Three Ways to Spend a GEO Budget


WebFX frames GEO budgets in three models: software only, a service with software included, and a service plus separate software. Software only is the cheapest line on paper. It still needs someone inside the company to read the data and act on it every week, and that time belongs in the budget. If you choose this route, our[guide to AI search performance tracking tools](https://www.geostar.ai/blog/ai-search-performance-tracking-tools-a-practitioner-s-guide-for-2026) covers how to evaluate them.


A full GEO budget, whichever model you choose, usually covers the six categories WebFX lists:


- AI visibility tracking
- Content optimization
- Technical improvements
- Competitor monitoring
- Reporting
- Internal execution time


The in-house comparison is where the totals separate. The pricing report puts a Growth-tier agency engagement at about $98,400 a year all-in, about 27% of the $363,512 cost of a three-person in-house team. That team figure rests on the dataset's own assumptions: median salaries of $96,400 for a GEO specialist and $74,600 for a content writer, plus benefits.


Tenpoint Labs recommends choosing between in-house, agency and hybrid by skills and available time, and comparing full cost including internal work. We agree. A team with strong writers and a developer on hand can get far with software and a consultant. A team without those people pays for the gap one way or another, either in hires or in work that never ships.


## Contract Terms That Protect a GEO Budget


None of the top-ranking pricing guides treats contract terms as their own topic, yet the contract decides what the monthly fee buys. Tenpoint Labs recommends four protections \[3\]. They are one agency's practice rather than an industry standard, and they are worth asking for:


1. A baseline visibility report as the first paid deliverable, owned by you.
2. The named prompts and the named AI engines in scope, written into the agreement.
3. The workstream split in writing, with the right to rebalance it quarterly.
4. Data portability on exit, so your prompt lists, baselines and reports leave with you.


Expect a minimum commitment as well. Minimum terms in the pricing data run 3 months at Starter, 6 months at Growth and Advanced, and 12 months at Enterprise, as the tier table above shows.


## How We Scope a GEO Engagement at Geostar


We do not publish a price for agency engagements, because a fixed menu would price work before anyone has looked at the site. Every[Geostar agency engagement](https://www.geostar.ai/agency) starts with a free audit, followed by prompt-space research that identifies the prompts and queries where you need to win.


From there, our team executes across content production, technical SEO and GEO implementation, and off-site citation work. The price is scoped to the audit findings. We do the work ourselves, and the monthly report shows what shipped.


If you are comparing GEO proposals now, an audit gives you a baseline to measure any of them against.[Book a free audit](https://www.geostar.ai/contact) .


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is GEO more expensive than SEO?


Yes, on current benchmarks. The First Page Sage dataset puts the median GEO/AEO retainer about 45% above the median SEO retainer, as covered in the tier section above. The report does not break down the cause. In our scoping, the difference comes from prompt tracking across several AI engines and a larger share of off-site authority work.


### How much should a small business budget for GEO?


Plan on roughly $1,500 to $5,000 a month for a basic agency program. WebFX gives that range for small businesses, and the Starter tier in the pricing report runs $1,800 to $4,200 with a median of $2,950 and a three-month minimum term. A one-off audit is a lower-cost way to set a baseline first.


### Is there a standard rate card for GEO?


No. Tenpoint Labs states that no established rate card exists, and only 23% of agencies in the pricing dataset publish any GEO pricing. Treat every published range as a directional benchmark, and compare proposals on platforms covered, prompts tracked, implementation and measurement rather than on the monthly figure alone.


### Can we run GEO in-house for less?


The vendor bill is lowest with software only, but the full cost includes the internal time to act on the data. Tenpoint Labs recommends comparing full cost, internal work included. Teams with writers and a developer already in place can keep costs low. Teams without them face hiring costs that the First Page Sage comparison puts well above a Growth-tier agency fee.
